about.title: Healdsburg Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Healdsburg's economy runs on wine, hospitality, and the trades that keep both running — vineyard crews, cellar workers, delivery drivers, hotel staff, and contractors moving equipment along Healdsburg Avenue and near US-101. When someone gets hurt on the job here, California law usually routes the claim through workers' compensation rather than a lawsuit against the employer. But that's not always the end of the story. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to the injury, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside the workers' comp claim. Sonoma County's mix of agricultural work, tourism, and construction means injury circumstances vary widely, and figuring out whether a third party bears responsibility takes a careful look at the facts. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect injured Healdsburg workers with an independent attorney who can review what happened, explain the options, and help move a claim forward without any upfront cost.

whyChoose.title: Why Injured Healdsburg Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: We Help Untangle Comp vs. Third-Party Claims
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against an employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can open a separate path to recovery. We connect you with an attorney who can sort out which claims apply to your situation.

items.title: We Know the Clock Matters
items.desc: Employer injury reports are generally due within 30 days, while a third-party injury claim carries a two-year deadline in California. Getting matched with an attorney early helps make sure neither deadline slips by.

items.title: We Understand Retaliation Concerns Are Real
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from punishing workers for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you're worried about retaliation, an independent attorney can advise you on your rights before you say anything to your employer.

items.question: I was hurt at a vineyard job near Dry Creek Road — can I still file a claim?
items.answer: Yes. Agricultural work is covered under California workers' compensation just like other jobs, so an injury there generally starts as a workers' comp claim. If equipment failure or a subcontractor's negligence played a role, there may also be grounds for a separate third-party claim. An attorney can look at the specifics of the job site and equipment involved.

items.question: Does it matter that Healdsburg is a small city with fewer employers than a big metro area?
items.answer: Not really — the size of the city doesn't change the underlying California law, which applies the same workers' comp rules and third-party claim options whether you work in a small operation or a large one. What matters more is the nature of the injury and who else, besides your employer, might share responsibility. An independent attorney can evaluate that regardless of company size.

items.question: What if my employer says I can't sue them for my injury?
items.answer: They're generally right that workers' comp is the exclusive remedy against an employer for a workplace injury, which is why most claims go through that system rather than a lawsuit. However, that doesn't shut the door on claims against other responsible parties, like equipment manufacturers or subcontractors. An attorney can explain whether your specific injury opens up any additional options.
